title: Acoustic relative positioning
description: Known sound signals and onboard microphone arrays give aerial robots a way to estimate where their teammates are and follow a leader.
introduction: Before compact LiDAR became part of the group's UAV platforms, sound offered another route to relative awareness. Robots emit known acoustic signals, listen with onboard microphone arrays, and use the resulting estimates to coordinate their motion.

problem.heading: Where is the other robot?
paragraphs: A team needs relative position information to act together. An aerial robot cannot always depend on GNSS or an external positioning installation to locate its neighbours.

The acoustic research asks whether signals produced by the robots themselves can provide useful relative observations through onboard sensing. It forms part of Meysam Basiri's earlier work on swarms of micro aerial vehicles.

approach.heading: Signal, listen and estimate.
paragraphs: Each sound-emitting robot produces a known acoustic signal. An onboard microphone array on another robot records that signal and supports relative bearing or position estimation.

In the leader–follower demonstration, the follower uses the acoustic estimate to follow the leader without GNSS or wireless state exchange. The associated RSS, ICRA and RA-L papers describe related stages of this research, with their own formulations and evaluations.

steps.text: Make the neighbouring aerial robot acoustically observable.

steps.title: Listen onboard
steps.text: Record the sound using a microphone array carried by the robot.

steps.title: Estimate relative state
steps.text: Use the acoustic observations to estimate bearing or position.

steps.title: Follow the leader
steps.text: Use relative awareness to guide the follower's motion.

evidence.label: Leader–follower hardware demonstration
evidence.text: The supplied experiment shows acoustic leader following using onboard sensing. The demonstration is attributed to the historical sound-based work, not to the later LiDAR localization methods.

evidence.label: A sequence of published methods
evidence.text: The linked 2013, 2014 and 2016 publications document distinct contributions to acoustic relative positioning and bearing estimation. Their results are kept with the corresponding papers rather than merged into a single performance claim.
